text:
Every month about 38,000 Meridian customers need to pay someone new and can't do it in the app. They phone us: eleven minutes a call, £7.40
  fully loaded, roughly £280k a month in the contact centre, and a queue that pushes our answer time past target every Monday. Around one in
  five hang up before the payee is set up. Some of those pay from another bank's app instead, and once a customer keeps a second current
  account for paying people, we lose the salary within a year. It is the top complaint in our app store reviews. Nobody dies; we slowly stop
  being the main account.

By phone or in branch. The customer calls, passes identity checks, reads out the sort code and account number, the agent runs the checks we
  are required to run, sets the payee up on the core banking platform and usually makes the first payment while they are on the line. It
  works, and it lets a trained person spot a customer who is being talked into something. The shortcomings: it takes eleven minutes and a
  queue, branch only works in opening hours and the contact centre is 7am to 10pm, it costs us £3.4m a year, and it is embarrassing for a bank
  whose whole pitch is the app.

Look it up: Look up Confirmation of Payee: what it is, who runs it, what results it returns, and what UK payment providers are required
     to do with a close match or a no match.
     Answer: Documented: identify the customer, capture the payee, run Confirmation of Payee, read the result to the customer, create the
     payee, take the first payment. As it runs: the customer often has the details on a text or an invoice and reads them wrong the first
     time, so the agent goes round twice. Confirmation of Payee comes back "close match" more often than "match" for sole traders because
     people give the trading name; the agent then has to explain what that means and the customer says "it's fine, send it". The agent asks
     which account to pay from and the customer frequently does not know what is in it, so the agent looks, and about one first payment in
     twenty is retried because the chosen account was short. And the step nobody documents: if the agent hears the customer being coached or
     reading from a script, they slow it down, ask why, and sometimes refuse. That stopped about 300 payments last year.

Three things. The core banking platform's payee-creation API, which the agent desktop already uses, has to be callable from the app
     channel with the same controls. The customer has to be able to complete it alone, including when Confirmation of Payee says something
     other than "match", without ringing us to ask what it means. And whatever replaces the agent's ear has to catch scams at least as well as
     the phone does, because moving this into the app removes the one human check we have.

Look it up: Look up Faster Payments irrevocability: whether a Faster Payment can be recalled once sent, and what the recovery route is
     when money goes to the wrong account or to a scammer.
     Answer: What has to be true: customers will finish the journey on their own, our fraud controls work without a person in the loop, and
     the platform holds up at peak. The riskiest is the second. A Faster Payment settles in seconds and cannot be recalled; once it has left,
     the only route is an indemnity request to the receiving bank, and we get back pennies in the pound. Today the agent is the last chance to
     stop a bad payment. We are assuming a screen can do that job. If it can't, every scam we used to catch on the phone becomes a loss.

The customer feels it, and the contact centre feels it every Monday. The budget sits with me as Head of Payments for the build, and the
     saving lands in Operations under a different director who has already counted it in next year's plan. So no, not the same person, and the
     fraud team holds a veto that neither of us funds: if losses rise they can stop the rollout. Those three have to be in the room.

A big idea worth a full cycle, and we have already spent the quick-fix budget on it twice: a call-back button and a form that emails the
     contact centre, both of which just moved the queue. It is the number one item on the app roadmap for the year. We would not redesign the
     whole payments area for it; it has to sit inside the existing pay flow, because the customers who need it most are the ones who never
     learn a new layout.

New technical work: payee creation from the app channel is new for us, though the API exists. Confirmation of Payee is already integrated
     server-side. New to everyone: an in-app scam intervention that we can later show a regulator was effective, and a record of what the
     customer saw. Assumptions about fit: that the same controls the agent desktop enforces can be applied to a customer session, and nobody
     has checked. A design we are assuming exists: a warning that stops a coached customer without stopping everyone else; the industry has
     not cracked that. Settle in advance: whether the first release puts a limit on the first payment to a new payee, and what it is. If we
     leave that open it will eat the cycle.

International and non-sterling payments. Business accounts. Standing orders, Direct Debits, scheduled or bulk payments. Payments started
     by a third-party app through Open Banking. Editing or deleting existing payees. Customers under 16. Changing the identity or login
     controls. This is: a personal customer, in our app, paying a new UK sort code and account number, once, now.

Look it up: Look up APP reimbursement in the UK: the Payment Systems Regulator's mandatory reimbursement rules for authorised push
      payment scams, who pays, the cap, the split between sending and receiving bank, the consumer standard of caution exception, and what the
      FCA's Consumer Duty requires of firms.
      Answer: Meridian is. Since October 2024 the sending bank reimburses authorised push payment scam losses up to the cap and splits it with
      the receiving bank; last year that was £2.1m gross for us. The only defence is that the customer ignored an effective warning, and we
      can only use it if we can show what they were shown and when. Internally, fraud operations own the claims, I own the journey, and
      Consumer Duty puts the outcome on the board. Our design does change who is accountable: on the phone, an agent who took a coached
      payment shares it; in the app there is no agent, so it is entirely ours unless the warning is one we can evidence.

Scam losses per thousand new payees above the phone baseline after the first month of the pilot, or a single loss over the reimbursement
      cap traceable to the journey. Below that, a completion rate under 70 per cent, because then we have built a more expensive way to
      generate a phone call. And a complaint rate on the new journey above the current app average. Any one of those and we go back to the
      phone for the affected segment.

Two metrics, two owners, one cohort. Fraud operations own confirmed scam losses per thousand new payees, measured against the phone
      baseline of the same months last year; pass is no worse. I own first-attempt completion, measured on the pilot cohort of 20,000
      customers; pass is 85 per cent finishing without a call. The set is every new-payee attempt in the pilot, not a sample, and both are
      read weekly in the same meeting.

Buy it: they are already asking; it is the top complaint and the reason people keep a second account. Use it: unproven, and the phone
      version needs a person to explain the name check result, so that is the risk. Build it: yes, the API and the checks exist; the new
      pieces are the intervention and the evidence, and the platform team have a quarter. Business: fraud operations are nervous and
      Operations want the saving; if the scam numbers hold everyone wins, and if they don't, it is my journey that gets switched off.

Everything the customer typed and everything they were shown, in order. The payee details as entered, the Confirmation of Payee request and result, every warning or
  message displayed with its timestamp, device and the customer's response, the account chosen, the amount, and the payment reference. Kept for six years, which is our
  existing retention for payment instructions and what a claims dispute or a complaint to the ombudsman would need.

Everything the customer typed and everything they were shown, in order. The payee details as entered, the Confirmation of Payee request and result, every warning or
  message displayed with its timestamp, device and the customer's response, the account chosen, the amount, and the payment reference. Kept for six years, which is our
  existing retention for payment instructions and what a claims dispute or a complaint to the ombudsman would need.

In the core banking platform in our two UK data centres, with the app tier in the UK region of our cloud provider. The name check sends the payee's sort code,
  account number and the name the customer typed to the receiving bank through Pay.UK's service and gets a result back; that is the only place the data goes. The
  privacy notice already says this because the phone journey uses the same path, and nothing leaves the UK.

Scope: a close-match or no-match name result, because that is most sole traders; paying your own account at another bank; joint accounts; a first payment retried
  because the account was short. Refusals we will say out loud: we will not send a payment to a new payee above the first-payment limit on day one; we will not let a
  customer skip the name check; we will not offer it for international or business payments in this release; and we will not stop a customer paying after a no-match,
  because it is their money and the rules do not let us, but we will not let them do it without having seen the result.

For the cost and demand: strong. Twelve months of contact-centre data, 38,000 calls a month, call listening on 200 of them, app-store reviews and twelve customer
  interviews. For whether an app can replace the agent on scams: weak. We have the phone team's 300 refusals and industry reports, and nothing of our own. The
  consequence of being wrong on the first is a business case that misses; on the second it is a reimbursement bill and a regulator. The evidence is proportionate to
  the first and not to the second, which is why the pilot is 20,000 customers and not everyone.

The name check has to come back inside two seconds at the 95th percentile, because a customer who waits longer assumes it failed and retries. The whole journey,
  details to payment sent, under three minutes for the median customer on a four-year-old Android phone on 4G outside London. Today nothing in the app is measured
  against that because the journey does not exist; the phone journey is eleven minutes, so the bar is not high.

Answer: Customers expect it to work at 11pm on a Sunday, because that is when they remember they owe someone. Peak is about 1,500 new-payee attempts an hour on a
  Friday evening once it is live. An hour down costs us roughly 1,500 phone calls or abandoned payments and a set of complaints; two hours down and it becomes a
  regulatory incident under our operational resilience tolerances. The payments platform team are paged, twenty-four hours, and I am on the call after thirty minutes.

Look it up (off-script box, before Submit): Look up WCAG 2.2: who publishes it, when it was published, what conformance level AA requires, and what changed between
  2.1 AA and 2.2 AA.

  Answer: WCAG 2.2 AA, the same as the rest of the app. Tested with VoiceOver and TalkBack, switch access, 200 per cent text, and with our disabled customer panel,
  because the people who most need to stop phoning us include those who find the phone hardest. The external accessibility partner audits before launch and the digital
  accessibility lead signs it off; it is a launch gate, not a follow-up.

The customer's authenticated session is the boundary. Nothing crosses it except the payee details going to the name check and the payment instruction going to the
  payments platform, both over existing bank channels. The attacker we design against is the person on the other end of the customer's phone call, coaching them
  through the screens in real time, and second, someone who has taken over the account. We refuse to store the full name returned by the name check beyond the match
  outcome, any screenshot or recording of the journey, and anything the customer typed into a warning beyond their response.
